strengths: Timely and practically significant topic: fully-quantized FP4 (NVFP4) pre-training of LLMs is an active area, and the paper pushes toward truly fully-4-bit training where NVIDIA's own recipe [12] falls back to BF16 for some blocks.

Well-designed technical contributions: the unbiased double-block quantization with forward/backward alignment (Xb alignment, stochastic rounding in backward, 1x16 weight group shape) is carefully reasoned, and Table 3a/3b ablations cleanly attribute gains to the 1x128 outer-block scaling and unbiased gradient estimation.

OsciReset is a simple, novel, and well-motivated solution to weight oscillation: the paper provides diagnostic evidence (Figs. 1-2, 6) for the phenomenon, compares against three prior oscillation-suppression baselines (Q-EMA, Freeze, Dampen) which all fail for LLMs (Fig. 5), and shows its own method works without hurting global optimization.

OutControl leverages the structural consistency of activation outliers (Fig. 3) for a static, training-aligned channel selection that works in both forward and backward, with a sensible ablation (Table 4) showing both components matter and 'largest norms' selection beats random.

Extensive pre-training evaluation from scratch on OLMo-2 at three scales (70M/150M/370M) and up to ~200B tokens, with perplexity plus ten downstream tasks and two PPL benchmarks; the method consistently beats Quartet and NVIDIA's recipe across settings (Tables 1-2, Fig. 4).
Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge small model/data scale and the lack of hardware to measure actual speedups, which is candid and appropriate.
weaknesses: Scale of evidence limits the claims: models are at most 370M parameters and 200B tokens, while the motivating application is billion-parameter LLM training. Quantization behavior (oscillation, outlier structure) may change qualitatively at larger scale, so the 51.3% gap-reduction headline number may not extrapolate.

No efficiency evaluation despite efficiency being the core motivation: throughput, memory, and the computational overhead of OsciReset (per-element statistics accumulation, Alg. 1-2) and OutControl (mixed-precision gather/scatter paths) are never quantified. Without this, the practical usefulness of the recipe is not established.

The 'fully FP4' framing is somewhat undermined by OutControl: 10% of activation channels are computed in FP8 (or 5% in BF16), which is the same type of mixed-precision concession the paper criticizes in NVIDIA's recipe, just at a finer granularity. The paper would benefit from explicitly quantifying this overhead and reconciling the framing.

Some ablations use inconsistent settings: e.g., Table 3a/3b use 50B tokens while 3c uses 100B, and Table 3c is on the 150M model while Table 1 is at 370M; Table 4 is on 150M. Cross-setting comparisons weaken the internal consistency of the evidence.

OsciReset introduces several hyperparameters (Tstart, Tperiod, Taccu, tau_osci) that are tuned per model size (Table 8, e.g., Tstart scales with total steps); the claim of 'little tuning of hyperparameters' is not fully substantiated, and no sensitivity analysis over these parameters is provided.

Small remaining gap to BF16: at 370M/200B, validation PPL is 25.11 vs 23.70 for BF16, and the average downstream accuracy is 43.60 vs 44.13; 'near-lossless' is not achieved and downstream gains over baselines are modest within seed-level noise (no error bars or repeated runs are reported).

The novelty is incremental relative to TetraJet [22]: the linear-layer design directly follows TetraJet's MXFP4 formulation, OsciReset follows its oscillation-detection scheme, and OutControl is inspired by LLM.int8(); the contribution is mainly adaptation of known ideas to NVFP4/LLM pre-training, which is valuable but should be stated more precisely.

Algorithmic details are underspecified for reproducibility of OutControl: how exactly outlier channels are selected 'at the starting stage of training' (based on which data, which statistic, how many steps) is not described; also, potential division-by-zero when distM(w)=0 in OsciRisk is not addressed, and code release is not mentioned.

strengths: Extensive pre-training experiments on OLMo-2 across three model sizes (70M/150M/370M) and up to ~200B tokens, with comparisons against recent state-of-the-art FP4 methods (Quartet, NVIDIA's NVFP4 recipe) and validation plus downstream evaluations (Tables 1–2, Fig. 4)

The identification and analysis of weight oscillation during LLM pre-training (Figs. 1–2, Fig. 6) is an interesting empirical observation, and the ablations comparing OsciReset against prior oscillation-suppression techniques (Q-EMA, Freeze, Dampen) are informative (Fig. 5)

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each design choice: outer-block scaling, weight group shape, gradient alignment, stochastic rounding, and Hadamard transform placement (Tables 3–4)
Useful loss-decomposition analyses (Tables 5–6) identifying activation quantization and MLP.ffn2 as bottlenecks, which provide actionable insight for future low-precision training work
Honest limitations section acknowledging the scale restriction and the inability to measure actual speedups
weaknesses: The central claim of 'accurate NVFP4 training for large language models' is not well supported at meaningful scale: experiments top out at 370M parameters and 200B tokens, far below the regime where FP4 training instabilities are known to be most severe. The gap to BF16 remains substantial (e.g., validation PPL 25.11 vs. 23.70 at 370M), so 'near-lossless' is far from demonstrated and scaling behavior is unknown

No efficiency evaluation whatsoever. The entire motivation for FP4 training is throughput and memory savings, yet the paper reports no speedup, memory, or overhead measurements — a critical omission given that OutControl routes 10% of channels through FP8/BF16 and OsciReset adds bookkeeping overhead, all of which may erode the theoretical FP4 gains

Downstream results are mixed and unconvincing: TetraJet-v2-full does not consistently beat baselines (e.g., ARC-c 24.75 vs. 26.76 for NVIDIA, lower PIQA and MMLU variance), improvements on the 10-benchmark average are modest (~0.8 points over NVIDIA), and no seed variance or significance testing is reported

The 'fully quantized' framing is oversold: outlier channels are retained in FP8, embeddings and non-linear components remain high precision, and the FP6×FP4 discussion further concedes that pure FP4×FP4 is insufficient

Limited novelty: the method is assembled from existing components (TetraJet's linear layer design, stochastic rounding, RHT from Quartet/mxfp4, LLM.int8()-style outlier retention, oscillation detection adapted from [20, 22]). OsciReset — resetting oscillating weights to bin centers — is simple but its hyperparameters (T_start, τ_osci, period) differ per model size, contradicting the 'little tuning' claim

Theoretical claims of unbiased gradient estimation and guaranteed SGD convergence are asserted by appeal to 'similar analysis in TetraJet' rather than stated or proven; the oscillation analysis rests on a single layer (blocks.11.att_proj of the 150M model)
No code release or clear reproducibility statement is provided, and baseline methods are run at 'default settings' without evidence of fair hyperparameter tuning across methods

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: fully 4-bit NVFP4 pre-training of LLMs, building directly on the newly introduced microscaling formats and the NVIDIA NVFP4 recipe [12].

The proposed OsciReset method is simple, novel in the LLM pre-training context, and well motivated: the oscillation phenomenon is clearly diagnosed (Figures 1-2, OsciRisk metric), and the reset-to-bin-center trick preserves the quantized model at the moment of reset, giving it an advantage over freezing or regularization-based approaches.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a quantization-training paper: pre-training of OLMo-2 at three model sizes (70M/150M/370M) on 50B-212B tokens, with both perplexity (Table 1) and a broad downstream benchmark suite (Table 2), against two relevant baselines (Quartet, NVIDIA recipe).

The ablation studies are comprehensive and support the design choices: outer-block scaling (Table 3a), forward/backward alignment and stochastic rounding (Table 3b), Hadamard transform placement (Table 3c), comparisons to prior oscillation-suppression methods (Figure 5), and loss decomposition identifying the activation quantizer and mlp.ffn2 as bottlenecks (Tables 5-6). These analyses have standalone value for future low-precision training work.
Limitations are discussed candidly (model scale, absence of hardware speedup evaluation), which is appropriate and honest.
Hyperparameters for all techniques and models are provided in the appendix, and the experiments build on the open OLMo codebase and public datasets, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central efficiency motivation is untested: the paper argues for FP4 training because of 'up to 3x higher compute performance and 2x lower memory usage,' but no throughput, memory, or kernel-level measurements are reported; the method is purely simulated. This is disclosed, but it means the practical payoff remains unverified, especially since components like OutControl (10% of channels in FP8 with separate high-precision matmuls) and OsciReset (periodic full-model statistics) add overheads whose real-world cost is unknown.

There is some tension with the paper's own positioning: the abstract/introduction emphasize that NVIDIA's recipe 'is not fully 4-bit' while TetraJet-v2 is 'end-to-end 4-bit ... in all linear layers,' yet TetraJet-v2-full retains 10% of activation channels in FP8 (OutControl) with high-precision multiplications in both forward and backward (the underlined red terms). This is a meaningful departure from a purely FP4 pipeline and deserves more direct acknowledgment.

The unbiasedness argument is informal. Stochastic rounding is unbiased per element, but gradients involve products of two independently quantized tensors (e.g., Q(dY) x Q(Wc)); the paper asserts unbiasedness 'according to a similar analysis in TetraJet [22]' and cites SGD convergence [30] without any formal statement or proof in this paper. A proof or at least a formal claim would strengthen the section.

Scale of evidence limits the claims: 370M parameters and ~200B tokens are far below the regime where FP4 recipes (e.g., NVIDIA's) are typically validated, and the oscillation phenomenon and outlier structure may change qualitatively at larger scales. The 51.3% gap-reduction figure is averaged over small models and may not extrapolate.

Downstream results are mixed: in Table 2 TetraJet-v2-full trails on several tasks (e.g., ARC-c 24.75 vs BF16 28.43 and vs its own base variant 27.75; MMLU 26.08 vs BF16 25.85 but below base variant in some entries), and the average improvement over baselines is modest (~0.8 points over Quartet). The residual gap to BF16 validation perplexity (e.g., 25.11 vs 23.70 at 370M) remains substantial.

Sensitivity of OsciReset to its hyperparameters (tau_osci, T_start, T_period) is not explored; results in Figures 4 and 7 use different T_start values across models, and the claim that the method 'needs little tuning' is not directly substantiated.

The theoretical contribution is thin (double-block scaling is a straightforward extension of block quantization; OsciReset is a heuristic), so the paper's originality rests mainly on the empirical analysis of oscillation in LLM pre-training and the recipe composition.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated identification of weight oscillation as a distinct failure mode of low-precision training, supported by empirical evidence (Fig. 1a/b distributions and trajectories) that goes beyond quantization-error arguments.

OsciReset is simple, novel for LLM pre-training, and convincingly ablated against prior oscillation-mitigation methods (Q-EMA, Freeze, Dampen in Fig. 4), with demonstrated robustness to its hyperparameters (Tables 9-10) and a memory-efficient variant (Table 7).

Extensive and careful experimental methodology: systematic ablations on block sizes, rounding schemes, and Hadamard transform placement (Table 8); loss decomposition analyses (Tables 3-4); expanded baselines (Table 12); Muon-optimizer compatibility (Table 13).

Real systems contribution: custom CUDA kernels with latency breakdowns, controlled overhead analysis of the 1x16 scaling scheme (Table 14), and end-to-end speedups on both transformer blocks (Fig. 9, Table 15) and full models (Table 16), measured against a TransformerEngine FP8 baseline with quantization overheads included.
Honest limitations section acknowledging the scale restriction (up to 370M params, 212B tokens), and reproducibility is aided by detailed hyperparameter tables (Tables 5-6) and a code release.
weaknesses: Scale limits the strength of central claims: experiments are on OLMo-2 models up to 370M parameters / 212B tokens, yet the abstract and framing advertise 'accurate NVFP4 training for LLMs.' Whether the oscillation dynamics and OsciReset benefits transfer to billion-scale models (where LR schedules, optimizer state magnitudes, and weight distributions differ) remains unverified, and the residual gap to BF16 is still substantial (e.g., 34.95 vs 33.49 at 150M).

The 'fully 4-bit' claim is qualified in practice: OutControl retains 10% of activation channels in FP8 in both forward and backward, so TetraJet-v2-full is not strictly fully FP4; while disclosed, the abstract's framing oversells this.

Theoretical support is thin relative to the language used: claims of 'practically optimal convergence,' 'rigorous theoretical derivation,' and unbiasedness lean on prior analyses (Chen et al. 2020, TetraJet) rather than new theory for the LLM/NVFP4 setting; no convergence proof or error analysis for OsciReset is provided.

Some experimental evidence is weak or noisy: downstream task differences in Table 2 are small (e.g., TetraJet-v2-full drops ARC-c from 27.75 to 24.75 relative to base) and the 370M scale is too small for reliable benchmark conclusions; the oscillation phenomenon is demonstrated mainly in the late, low-LR phase, so the practical scope of OsciReset may be narrow.

Efficiency results are on consumer GPUs (RTX 5090/6000 Pro) rather than datacenter Blackwell hardware where NVFP4 would actually be deployed, and the FP8 baseline's configuration could favor the comparison; the 1.67x headline speedup is for the transformer-layer forward/backward, with full-model system-level integration (communication, optimizer, data loading) not addressed.

Presentation issues: the code link in the abstract is blank; the loss-decomposition conclusion (Table 3) that quantizing dW alone is 'lossless' (−0.01) is surprising and not explained; minor typos ('mix-precision', 'FQT' expansion inconsistency) suggest incomplete proofreading.

strengths: Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 8, 9, 10, 11) that isolate the contribution of each design choice: outer-block scaling, weight group shape, stochastic rounding/activation alignment, and per-MM Hadamard placement, which strengthens the empirical support for the linear-layer design.

Detailed reproduction information: model and training hyperparameters (Table 5), method hyperparameters (Table 6), algorithms in pseudocode, and memory/latency overhead analysis (Table 7, App. C.2), plus a code release commitment.

Well-motivated empirical characterization of weight oscillation (Fig. 1) with a useful analysis of the oscillation-vs-quantization-error relationship (App. C.3) and evidence that prior ViT-oriented oscillation mitigations (Q-EMA, Freeze, Dampen) fail at LLM training regimes (Fig. 4).

Practical efficiency work: real CUDA kernels with measured end-to-end speedups on consumer/datacenter GPUs (Figs. 5, 8, 9, Tables 15, 16), including full-model measurements, rather than theoretical FLOP counts alone.
Verification of robustness across optimizers (Muon compatibility, Table 13) and against several recent FP4 baselines (Table 12), and an honest limitations section acknowledging the scale constraint.
weaknesses: Scale of experiments undermines the central claims about 'LLM training': the largest model is 370M parameters (474M with embeddings). Weight-oscillation dynamics, outlier structure, and the effectiveness of a periodic reset scheme may change qualitatively at 1B-100B+ scale, where the practical motivation lies. The '500-600x tokens-per-parameter' regime partially compensates, but the paper offers no evidence the recipe transfers to larger models.

The 'fully 4-bit' framing is weakened by OutControl: 10% of activation channels are retained in FP8 in both forward and backward passes (Table 6, Sec. 4.2). The headline claim of 'end-to-end 4-bit FQT' is therefore a mixed-precision method, and the paper does not clearly report how much of the accuracy gain comes from this FP8 fallback versus the novel components.

Novelty of the individual components is modest: OsciReset is a simple variant of oscillation handling from Nagel et al. (2022) and Chen et al. (2025) (reset to bin center instead of freeze/EMA), OutControl closely follows LLM.int8()-style static outlier-channel retention, and the Hadamard/stochastic-rounding components are standard. The claim of being 'the first effective algorithm to suppress LLMs' weight oscillation' is stated but the delta over TetraJet (Chen et al., 2025) is incremental.

Overclaimed theoretical rigor: the discussion asserts 'rigorous theoretical derivation' and 'practically optimal convergence,' but the main paper contains only a short unbiasedness argument for stochastic rounding, no convergence proof, and no theoretical treatment of OsciReset's effect on optimization.

Some headline metrics are presented favorably without standard error analysis: no seed variance or confidence intervals for any perplexity result, and downstream benchmark gaps (Table 2) are within noise for many tasks (e.g., MMLU 25.10 vs 26.08, OBQA differences below 1 point), while Table 1's '51.3% average gap reduction' is computed only on perplexity.

Several key design choices are justified only empirically (RHT harmful in forward, RHT helping dX, static outlier selection at 1% of training), with limited mechanistic explanation, which limits generalizability beyond the tested OLMo-2 architecture and dataset.

strengths: Thorough and well-scoped empirical evaluation: three OLMo-2 model sizes (70M/150M/370M) trained on substantial token budgets (up to 212B tokens, ~500-600 TPP), with perplexity, ten downstream benchmarks, and expanded baseline comparisons in App. E (Quartet, NVIDIA recipe, Tseng et al., Wang et al., FourOverSix), consistently showing TetraJet-v2 ahead of all FP4 baselines.

OsciReset is a genuinely interesting contribution: the paper convincingly demonstrates and characterizes weight oscillation in LLM FP4 pre-training (Fig. 1), shows prior ViT-oriented oscillation remedies (Q-EMA, Freeze, Dampen) fail in this regime (Fig. 4), and proposes a simple reset-to-bin-center fix that is robust to hyperparameter choices (Tabs. 9-10) and validated by oscillation-proportion measurements (Fig. 7) and the oscillator/quantization-error analysis in App. C.3.

Practical relevance is well supported: real CUDA kernels with full overhead accounting (quantization, de-quantization, Hadamard) showing 1.67-1.75x end-to-end speedup over TransformerEngine FP8 (Figs. 5, 8, 9, Tab. 15-16), plus a memory-efficient oscillation-tracking variant (~0.6 bytes/param) with measured overhead (Tab. 7).

Extensive and transparent ablations (Tabs. 3-4, 8, 11) that isolate the contribution of each design choice (block shapes, stochastic rounding, alignment, per-MM Hadamard placement), and useful analyses such as loss decomposition and FP6×FP4 hybrid-precision exploration.
Reproducibility is strong: complete hyperparameter tables (Tab. 5-6), detailed algorithms (Alg. 1-4), promised code release, and an honest limitations section acknowledging the modest model scale.
weaknesses: Scale limitation materially weakens the central claims: all results are on models up to 370M parameters. Low-precision training behavior (oscillation dynamics, outlier structure, LR-schedule interaction) can change qualitatively at the multi-billion-parameter scale where FP4 training actually matters, and the paper's framing of general 'LLM training' conclusions outpaces the evidence. The limitations discussion acknowledges this but the title/abstract claims are not correspondingly hedged.

Significant residual gap to BF16 remains (e.g., 370M val PPL 25.11 vs 23.70; Wiki PPL 18.06 vs 16.86), and downstream gains are mixed: TetraJet-v2-full regresses on ARC-c (24.75 vs BF16's 28.43 and even below the base variant's 27.75) and several other benchmarks, with only a modest average improvement (43.60 vs 42.77/43.41). No seed variance or significance testing is reported for any perplexity or accuracy numbers.

Incrementality relative to TetraJet (Chen et al., 2025) is substantial: the six-matrix quantized linear design, oscillation detection metric (distQ/distM), and stochastic-rounding analysis are all inherited from prior work; the core novelty reduces to adapting these to NVFP4/LLMs, the reset-based suppression rule, and static outlier-channel retention (itself inspired by LLM.int8()). The 'rigorous theoretical derivation' claimed in Sec. 6.1 is not present in the manuscript; convergence claims rest on citations to prior analyses.

The 'fully 4-bit' framing is somewhat undermined by OutControl, which retains ~10% of activation channels in FP8 (or higher) in both forward and backward; calling the resulting recipe fully NVFP4 training requires qualification, and the sensitivity of results to the outlier ratio p is not ablated.

The NVIDIA baseline was modified (a mixed-precision recipe forced into a fully-4-bit setting it was not designed for), which, while justified for fairness, complicates interpretation of that comparison; and all efficiency measurements are on consumer GPUs (RTX 5090/6000 Pro) rather than the Blackwell datacenter hardware where NVFP4 tensor cores actually ship, leaving the claimed 1.67x speedup unverified on target hardware.

Overclaiming in places: 'practically optimal convergence', 'the currently optimal fully-FP4 configuration', and 'the first effective algorithm' are stronger than the evidence (empirical tuning over two model scales) supports.
